title: Blockchain Fundamentals: Blocks, Hashing & Consensus
tagline: Go under the hood: tamper with blocks, hash live, mine and compare proof of work, stake and BFT
summary: A rigorous but friendly look at the core machinery of blockchains: block and transaction structure, cryptographic hashes and Merkle trees, proof of work and its economics, proof of stake and BFT voting, forks and finality, and how to design and critique consensus. Live labs let you hash, tamper, mine and calculate.

modules.title: Blocks and transactions
modules.summary: The anatomy of a block, how a transaction is built, and the journey from wallet to confirmed record.
modules.outcome: You can name the parts of a block, explain UTXO and account models and trace a transaction through the network.
modules.intro: Before looking at hashing and consensus, you need a precise picture of the objects involved. This module takes a block and a transaction apart so that every later idea has something solid to attach to.

topics.title: Anatomy of a block
topics.html:
A block has two parts. The body holds the list of transactions. The header is a small summary that the network hashes. Keeping the header small means that checking a block's validity and linking blocks together does not require handling all of the transaction data.

A typical block header (Bitcoin-style)
FieldJob
VersionWhich rules the block follows
Previous block hashLinks the block to its parent
Merkle rootA single hash that commits to every transaction in the body
TimestampApproximate time of creation
Difficulty targetHow small a valid hash must be
NonceA number that miners change to try different hashes

The block's own hash is computed from the header. Because the header contains the Merkle root, changing any transaction changes the root, then the header, then the block hash, and then breaks the next block's link.

Check what you just learned

1. Which field lets a block commit to all of its transactions with one short value?
  • Nonce
  • Timestamp
  • Merkle root (correct)
  • Version

The root is a hash over all transaction hashes.

Tip

Think of the header as the cover page and the transactions as the pages. The cover carries a fingerprint of all the pages, and each cover also carries the fingerprint of the previous book.

Check what you just learned

1. Which field changes when any transaction in the block changes?
  • Version
  • Block size limit
  • Timestamp
  • Merkle root (correct)

The root is built from the transactions.

2. The next block stores:
  • The previous block's hash (correct)
  • The previous block's transactions
  • Your password
  • The miner's phone number

That is the chain link.
keyPoints: The header is a compact summary; the body holds the transactions.
The Merkle root ties every transaction to the header.

topics.title: Transactions: UTXOs and accounts
topics.html:
Blockchains keep track of who owns what in one of two main ways.

Two accounting models
UTXO model (Bitcoin)Account model (Ethereum)
IdeaCoins are separate outputs, like banknotes: you spend whole outputs and get changeEach address has a balance, like a bank account
SpendingA transaction lists the outputs it consumes and creates new onesA transaction reduces one balance and increases another
Double-spend checkAn output can be spent once; the network tracks the unspent setA counter called a nonce orders each account's transactions
StrengthsSimple to verify in parallel; good privacy habits possibleNatural for smart contracts and balances
Worked example

A UTXO payment

Asha owns one output worth 10 coins and pays Ben 3 coins with a fee of 0.1.

  1. The transaction consumes the 10-coin output.
  2. It creates a 3-coin output for Ben.
  3. It creates a 6.9-coin output back to Asha as change.
  4. The difference of 0.1 is the fee, collected by the miner.

Answer. Outputs are spent whole, which is why change outputs exist.

Formula · Conservation rule

sum of inputs = sum of outputs + fee

Every valid transaction must satisfy this; nodes reject any that create value from nothing.

Check what you just learned

1. In the UTXO model, what happens to the unspent remainder when you pay less than an output's full value?
  • It is burned
  • It returns to you as a new 'change' output (correct)
  • It goes to the miner automatically
  • It stays in the old output

Outputs are consumed whole, so change is a new output.

Check what you just learned

1. A 'change output' exists because:
  • It is a bug
  • Fees are refunded
  • Outputs are spent whole (correct)
  • Wallets are slow

You must consume the full output.
keyPoints: UTXO chains track unspent outputs; account chains track balances.
Inputs always equal outputs plus fee.

topics.title: From wallet to confirmed block
topics.html:
What each stage checks
StageChecks
WalletEnough balance; correct address; fee set
NodeValid signature; funds not already spent; format and size; fee above the minimum
Block producerChooses transactions, often by fee, and fits them within the block limit
Other nodesRe-check every transaction in the block and the header link before accepting

The mempool is each node's waiting room of valid, unconfirmed transactions. When the network is busy, low-fee transactions can wait a long time, and wallets let you raise the fee to jump the queue. A confirmation is each additional block built on top of the one that contains your transaction.

Throughput and waiting

Change the block size, the transaction size and the block time to see how many transactions fit per block and per second.

Adjust Block size (bytes), Average transaction (bytes), Block time (seconds) and see Transactions per block, Transactions per second change.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the mempool?
  • The set of mined blocks
  • A mining pool
  • A wallet backup
  • A node's waiting room of valid unconfirmed transactions (correct)

Transactions wait there until included.

Check what you just learned

1. A confirmation is:
  • One more block built on top of your transaction's block (correct)
  • An email from the wallet
  • A signature
  • A fee

More blocks mean more certainty.

Key terms: flip and sort

Block header
The compact summary of a block that is hashed
Merkle root
One hash that commits to all transactions
Nonce
A number miners vary to find a valid hash
UTXO
Unspent transaction output
Mempool
A node's pool of unconfirmed transactions
Confirmation
A block built on top of a transaction's block
keyPoints: A transaction is signed, broadcast, held in the mempool, mined and then confirmed.
Fees decide priority when blocks are full.

modules.title: Hashing in depth
modules.summary: What makes a hash function cryptographic, how Merkle trees compress thousands of transactions into one value, and what else hashes do in a blockchain.
modules.outcome: You can state the properties of a cryptographic hash, use a hash to detect tampering and explain how a Merkle proof works.
modules.intro: Hashing is the most used tool in blockchains. It builds the links between blocks, summarises transactions, creates addresses and powers mining. A solid grasp of its properties lets you reason about security claims instead of memorising them.

topics.title: Properties of a cryptographic hash
topics.html:
The properties
PropertyPlain meaningWhat breaks if it fails
DeterministicSame input, same hashNodes could not agree on a block's identity
Fast to computeHashing is cheapChecking blocks would be too slow
Preimage resistanceGiven a hash, you cannot find an input that produces itAttackers could forge data for a known fingerprint
Second-preimage resistanceGiven one input, you cannot find a different input with the same hashA transaction could be swapped for another
Collision resistanceYou cannot find any two inputs with the same hashTwo different histories could look identical
Avalanche effectTiny changes produce unrelated hashesEdits would leave visible patterns

Try the lab to see determinism and the avalanche effect first-hand. Notice that a one-letter change affects roughly half of the 256 bits.

Hash anything

Type a sentence, then change one character. Compare the number of bits that changed.

Type any text and see its SHA-256 fingerprint change completely when one letter changes.

How big is 2^256?

Change the number of bits to see how the number of possible hash values grows. Each extra bit doubles it. (The numbers become astronomically large; the chart shows powers of ten.)

Adjust Hash length in bits, Guesses per second and see Possible hashes, Seconds to try them all change.

Watch out

Hash functions age. MD5 and SHA-1 were once common and are now considered broken for security uses because researchers found practical collisions. Blockchains use modern functions such as SHA-256 and Keccak-256, and a design should allow for replacement.

Check what you just learned

1. Which property says that it is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same hash?
  • Determinism
  • Collision resistance (correct)
  • Speed
  • Avalanche effect

A collision is two inputs with one hash.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does a block explorer show you the same hash as your node?
  • It copies it
  • Hashes are random
  • Hashing is deterministic (correct)
  • They share a password

Everyone computes the same output.

2. A hash that can be reversed would:
  • Be better
  • Be illegal
  • Be faster
  • Let attackers forge data from fingerprints (correct)

One-way is essential.
keyPoints: A cryptographic hash is deterministic, fast, one-way and collision resistant.
Old hash functions such as MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for security.

topics.title: Merkle trees and proofs
topics.html:
A block may hold thousands of transactions, but the header holds just one 32-byte value that commits to all of them. That value is the Merkle root, produced by a tree of hashes: hash every transaction, then hash pairs of hashes, then pairs of those, until one hash remains.

Change a transaction, watch the root

Edit any transaction. The red hashes are the ones that changed. Everything else stays the same.

8 transactions are hashed in pairs up to one Merkle root. Change one transaction and the root changes.

Definition

Merkle proof. The short list of sibling hashes needed to recompute the root from one transaction. If the recomputed root matches the one in the block header, the transaction is in that block.

Formula · Size of a proof

proof length = log₂(number of transactions)

A block with 1,024 transactions needs only 10 hashes in a proof; one with about a million needs 20.

Why this matters

  • Light clients, such as phone wallets, can check that a payment is in a block without downloading every transaction.
  • Any tampering with a transaction changes the root, so the block header no longer matches.
  • Large sets of data can be summarised and checked cheaply, which is useful far beyond payments.

Check what you just learned

1. If you change one transaction, which hashes change?
  • That leaf and every hash on the path to the root (correct)
  • Only that leaf
  • None
  • All hashes in the tree

Only the path changes, but the root changes.

Check what you just learned

1. A Merkle proof lets you:
  • Mine faster
  • Prove a transaction is in a block without the whole block (correct)
  • Reverse a hash
  • Sign a message

Light clients rely on it.
keyPoints: A Merkle root commits to all transactions in a block.
A proof is about log₂(n) hashes long.

topics.title: Other jobs hashes do
topics.html:
Hashes across a blockchain system
UseHow
Linking blocksEach header contains the previous header's hash
Transaction identifiersA transaction's hash is its ID
AddressesAddresses are derived by hashing public keys, which shortens them and adds a layer of protection
CommitmentsPublish a hash now to prove later that you knew a value, without revealing it
Proof of workFind a nonce so the header's hash is below the target
Storage integrityVerify that a file retrieved from elsewhere matches its expected hash
Worked example

A commit and reveal

Two players want to choose a secret number fairly without seeing each other's choice first.

  1. Each writes a number plus a random secret string.
  2. Each publishes only the hash of 'number + secret'.
  3. After both have published, each reveals the number and secret.
  4. Anyone can hash the reveal and check that it matches the earlier commitment.

Answer. The hash binds you to your choice without disclosing it.

Common mistakes

  • Calling hashing 'encryption'. Encryption can be reversed with a key; a hash cannot.
  • Hashing very short, guessable inputs and assuming they are safe. An attacker can try all small inputs.
  • Using a fast hash on its own to store passwords; password systems add salt and deliberately slow functions.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a commit-and-reveal scheme used for?
  • Mining
  • Hiding transactions forever
  • Committing to a value now and revealing it later without changing it (correct)
  • Setting fees

The hash is a binding promise.

Check what you just learned

1. An address is usually derived by:
  • Counting blocks
  • Hashing the private key
  • Encrypting the balance
  • Hashing the public key (correct)

Hashing shortens and protects the key.

Key terms: flip and sort

Cryptographic hash
A one-way function producing a fixed-size fingerprint
Preimage
An input that produces a given hash
Collision
Two different inputs with the same hash
Merkle tree
A tree of hashes ending in one root
Merkle proof
The sibling hashes needed to check inclusion
Commitment
A hash that locks in a value without revealing it
keyPoints: Hashes link blocks, identify transactions, make addresses and enable commitments.
A hash is not encryption.

modules.title: Proof of work
modules.summary: The mining puzzle, how difficulty adjusts, what mining costs, and how much protection work really gives.
modules.outcome: You can explain the proof-of-work puzzle, estimate expected mining time, describe difficulty adjustment and reason about attacks.
modules.intro: Proof of work is the mechanism that secured Bitcoin from the start. It turns computing effort into a vote that cannot be faked. This module goes from the puzzle itself to the economics and the attacks it is designed to resist.

topics.title: The mining puzzle
topics.html:
A miner assembles a candidate block, including a coinbase transaction that pays the miner the block reward, then hashes the block header repeatedly, changing the nonce each time. A block is valid only if the hash, read as a very large number, is below a target. Since hashes are effectively random, the only way to find one is to try many nonces.

Mine a chain at different difficulties

Increase the difficulty, edit a block and press 'Re-link and mine'. Notice how the number of tries grows.

A chain of 3 linked blocks. Change the data in one block and see every later block break until it is mined again.

Formula · Expected work

expected hashes ≈ 2 ^ (number of leading zero bits required)

Requiring 20 leading zero bits needs about 1,048,576 tries on average; 32 bits needs about 4.3 billion.

Finding a valid nonce is hard, but checking one is trivial: a single hash. That asymmetry is the heart of proof of work. The block itself is the proof that someone did the work.

Check what you just learned

1. Why is a proof of work easy to verify?
  • Because checking needs just one hash of the block (correct)
  • Because it is encrypted
  • Because a bank confirms it
  • Because it is short

Verification is one hash; finding it takes many.

Tip

Two practical points: miners are free to choose any nonce, and the winning hash is not 'special' beyond meeting the target. No clever shortcut exists beyond faster hardware.

Check what you just learned

1. Each extra required zero bit makes mining about:
  • Half as hard
  • Twice as hard (correct)
  • The same
  • Ten times easier

Work doubles.
keyPoints: A valid block's hash must be below a target.
Finding a nonce is costly; verifying it is cheap.

topics.title: Difficulty and incentives
topics.html:
If more miners join, blocks would be found faster and faster. To keep a steady pace, the network adjusts the target regularly. Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, aiming for about ten minutes per block, which is about two weeks.

Formula · Difficulty adjustment (idea)

new target = old target × (actual time for the last 2,016 blocks ÷ expected time)

If the last 2,016 blocks took less time than planned, the target shrinks and puzzles get harder.

Mining time for a single miner

Change the required zero bits and the hash rate. This is a simplified teaching model.

Adjust Leading zero bits required, Hash rate (hashes per second) and see Expected tries, Expected seconds change.

Why miners take part
RewardSource
Block subsidyNew coins created in each block, halving every 210,000 blocks on Bitcoin
Transaction feesPaid by users to have transactions included

Miners spend on hardware and electricity, so they will keep mining only while the expected reward exceeds their cost. That connects the coin's price, fees and the total hash rate, and it is why the network's security depends on its economics.

Check what you just learned

1. Why does the network adjust difficulty?
  • To raise prices
  • To punish miners
  • To keep the average block time steady as total hash power changes (correct)
  • To reduce fees to zero

Steady block times need a moving target.

Check what you just learned

1. If lots of new miners join, difficulty will:
  • Fall
  • Be deleted
  • Stay the same forever
  • Rise (correct)

Blocks would otherwise come too fast.
keyPoints: Difficulty adjusts to keep a steady block time.
Miners are paid with block subsidy and fees.

topics.title: Attacks and how much safety work buys
topics.html:
Definition

51% attack. An attack in which one party controls a majority of the network's hash power and can therefore privately build a longer chain and release it to reorganise recent blocks, for example to reverse its own payments (a double spend). It cannot steal other people's coins or break signatures.

What an attacker can and cannot do
CanCannot
Reverse its own recent transactionsSpend coins it does not own
Block some transactions from being confirmedChange old history without redoing all the work since
Pause confirmations for othersCreate coins beyond the rules
Formula · Catching up (simplified)

chance ≈ (q ÷ p) ^ z

q is the attacker's share, p = 1 − q, and z is the number of blocks the attacker is behind. When q < p the chance falls exponentially with z.

How safe are z confirmations?

Change the attacker's share and the confirmations. The result is the simplified chance of ever catching up.

Adjust Attacker share of hash power (%), Confirmations and see Chance of catching up change.

Watch out

Small chains with little hash power have suffered real 51% attacks, because renting enough power temporarily can be cheap. A well-known name is no guarantee of security; check how much work protects a chain.

Check what you just learned

1. What can a 51% attacker NOT do?
  • Steal coins protected by other people's private keys (correct)
  • Reverse its own recent payments
  • Delay some transactions
  • Pause confirmations

Signatures still protect everyone's coins.

Check what you just learned

1. A 51% attacker cannot:
  • Double spend its own coins
  • Forge other people's signatures (correct)
  • Delay transactions
  • Build a longer chain

Signatures remain secure.

Key terms: flip and sort

Target
The threshold a valid block hash must fall below
Difficulty
How hard it is to find a valid hash
Hash rate
Hashes tried per second
Block subsidy
New coins paid to the block producer
Coinbase transaction
The special first transaction paying the miner
51% attack
Control of a majority of hash power
keyPoints: A majority of hash power can reorder recent blocks, not steal coins.
More confirmations make a catch-up attack exponentially less likely.

modules.title: Proof of stake and other mechanisms
modules.summary: How validators replace miners, why slashing matters and when voting-style consensus is a better fit.
modules.outcome: You can explain proof of stake, slashing and finality, and compare PoS and BFT-style voting with proof of work.
modules.intro: Proof of work secures a chain with electricity. Other designs secure it with money at stake or with a known group of voters. Each choice changes who can take part, how fast blocks are final and what attacks cost.

topics.title: Proof of stake
topics.html:
In proof of stake, participants called validators lock up coins as a deposit (a stake). The protocol selects validators to propose and attest to blocks, with a chance roughly proportional to their stake. Honest validators earn rewards; dishonest ones can lose part of their deposit.

Compared with proof of work
Proof of workProof of stake
Scarce resourceComputing power and electricityLocked coins
Cost of an attackRent or buy hardware and energy; costs can be recovered by selling hardwareAcquire a large stake that may be destroyed by slashing
Energy useHighVery low
RewardsBlock subsidy and fees to minersStaking rewards and fees to validators
Concentration riskMining pools and hardware makersLarge holders and staking services
Definition

Slashing. A penalty in which a validator that provably misbehaves, for example by signing two conflicting blocks, loses part or all of its stake and is removed.

A validator's yearly reward

Change the stake, reward rate and commission to see what is earned. These are teaching numbers.

Adjust Stake (coins), Yearly reward rate (%), Slash fraction (%) and see Yearly reward (coins), Loss if slashed (coins), Years of rewards to recover a slash change.

Check what you just learned

1. What is the main thing a validator risks in proof of stake?
  • Electricity bills
  • Its wallet app
  • Part of its deposited stake if it cheats (correct)
  • Block time

That is what slashing enforces.

Check what you just learned

1. Slashing punishes:
  • Honest validators
  • Wallets
  • Users with high fees
  • Provable misbehaviour (correct)

It makes cheating costly.
keyPoints: Validators lock stake and earn rewards; cheaters can be slashed.
PoS uses far less energy but can concentrate influence.

topics.title: Finality and voting-based consensus
topics.html:
Definition

Finality. The guarantee that a block will not be reversed. Proof of work offers probabilistic finality: the deeper a block is buried, the safer it is. Voting protocols can offer absolute finality once enough validators have signed.

Byzantine fault tolerant (BFT) protocols come from the study of how a group of computers can reach agreement when some of them may be faulty or malicious. In a classic design with n validators, agreement is guaranteed as long as fewer than one third are faulty, so 4 validators tolerate 1 fault and 7 tolerate 2.

Formula · BFT fault tolerance

faults tolerated f = floor((n − 1) ÷ 3), quorum = 2f + 1

With n = 10, f = 3 and a quorum of 7 signatures is needed.

When each family fits
SettingGood fitWhy
Open, anonymous participantsPoW or PoSCost or deposit replaces identity
A consortium of known organisationsBFT-style votingIdentified, accountable, fast finality
A single trusted ownerA databaseNo need for consensus

Check what you just learned

1. With 10 validators in a classic BFT design, how many faulty ones can be tolerated?
  • 3 (correct)
  • 1
  • 5
  • 9

floor((10-1)/3) = 3.

Tip

Choose the cheapest mechanism that gives the trust you need. A permissioned group does not need to burn electricity to agree.

Check what you just learned

1. How many faulty nodes can 7 validators tolerate in classic BFT?
  • 1
  • 2 (correct)
  • 3
  • 7

floor(6/3) = 2.
keyPoints: BFT-style voting gives immediate finality with known validators.
With n validators, f = floor((n − 1)/3) faults are tolerated.

topics.title: The trilemma and trade-offs
topics.html:
The blockchain trilemma says that it is hard to get all three of decentralisation, security and scalability at once. Improving one usually costs another.

Common trade-offs
ChoiceGainsCosts
Bigger blocks or faster blocksMore throughputHeavier hardware needs push out small nodes and reduce decentralisation
Fewer validatorsSpeed and simple coordinationEasier to collude or attack
Layer 2 rollupsCheap fast transactions that inherit base-layer securityMore complexity and new trust assumptions
Permissioned networkSpeed, privacy and accountabilityNot open; relies on the members' honesty

Questions to ask about any chain's consensus

  • Who can propose and validate blocks?
  • What does it cost to attack, and can the attacker recover the cost?
  • How quickly is a block final?
  • What happens if a majority is dishonest?
  • How decentralised is the validator set in practice, not just in theory?

Check what you just learned

1. Fewer validators usually means:
  • Less speed
  • More security always
  • Faster agreement but easier collusion (correct)
  • No finality

Fewer parties coordinate faster but can also collude.

Key terms: flip and sort

Validator
A participant that stakes coins to propose and attest to blocks
Stake
Coins locked as a deposit
Slashing
Penalty for provable misbehaviour
BFT
Byzantine fault tolerance
Quorum
The number of votes needed to decide
Trilemma
The tension between decentralisation, security and scalability
keyPoints: Decentralisation, security and scalability pull against each other.
Ask who controls block production in practice.

modules.title: Forks, reorganisations and finality
modules.summary: What happens when the network disagrees, how it heals, and how many confirmations are enough.
modules.outcome: You can explain temporary forks, soft and hard forks, reorganisations and how to decide how long to wait for a payment.
modules.intro: A distributed network does not always agree instantly. Messages take time to travel, two valid blocks can appear at once, and communities sometimes disagree about the rules. Understanding forks lets you read news about chain splits and pay safely.

topics.title: Temporary forks and reorganisations
topics.html:
Because nodes are spread across the world, two miners may each find a valid block at almost the same moment. Different nodes see different blocks first, so the network briefly has two competing tips. The next block built on one of them breaks the tie: nodes follow the chain with the most accumulated work, and the losing block becomes an orphan (or stale block).

Definition

Reorganisation (reorg). When nodes replace the last few blocks of their chain with a different, heavier branch. Transactions in the dropped blocks go back to the mempool and are usually confirmed again in the new branch, but a conflicting one can win instead.

Why a few confirmations matter
ConfirmationsMeaning
0 (in the mempool)The transaction can still be replaced or never confirmed
1In a block, but a one-block reorg is plausible
6Deeply buried on a large proof-of-work network; reversal needs an enormous share of hash power

Check what you just learned

1. What happens to the block that loses a temporary fork?
  • It is kept forever as the main chain
  • It becomes a smart contract
  • It is deleted from the internet
  • It becomes an orphan and its transactions return to the mempool (correct)

Valid transactions are usually included again.

Check what you just learned

1. Nodes choose between competing chains by:
  • Most accumulated work (correct)
  • Random choice
  • Newest timestamp only
  • Largest file

Heaviest chain rule.
keyPoints: Temporary forks heal as nodes follow the chain with the most work.
Waiting for confirmations protects against reorganisations.

topics.title: Soft forks, hard forks and chain splits
topics.html:
Deliberate rule changes
TypeWhat changesEffect on old nodesExample idea
Soft forkRules become stricterOld nodes still accept new blocksAdding a new transaction type that old nodes treat as valid but ignore
Hard forkRules are loosened or changedOld nodes reject new blocks and split off if they do not upgradeIncreasing block size or changing the consensus mechanism

A hard fork can be planned and peaceful, where everyone upgrades by an agreed block height, or contentious, where part of the community refuses and continues the old rules. A contentious hard fork produces two chains with a shared history up to the split and separate histories afterwards.

What to do when a chain splits

  1. Do not rush to move funds on either chain until wallets and exchanges announce support.
  2. Beware of 'replay attacks', where a transaction valid on both chains is repeated on the other.
  3. Check the announcements of your wallet and exchange.
  4. Expect scam airdrops and phishing sites to appear during splits.

Check what you just learned

1. A soft fork is best described as:
  • A rule change that old nodes reject
  • A tightening of rules that old nodes still accept (correct)
  • A bug
  • A new coin sale

Backward compatible.

Watch out

Forks create confusion that scammers exploit. Rely on official sources and avoid links in messages.

Check what you just learned

1. A hard fork requires:
  • Nothing
  • Fewer miners
  • Nodes to upgrade or be left on a separate chain (correct)
  • No agreement

Old software rejects the new blocks.
keyPoints: Soft forks tighten rules and stay compatible; hard forks loosen or change them and can split the chain.
Be careful during splits: replay attacks and scams.

topics.title: Deciding how long to wait
topics.html:
There is no single right number of confirmations. The answer depends on the value at stake, the size and health of the chain, and how quickly you must act.

A practical guide (teaching rule of thumb)
SituationSuggested approach
A small purchase on a large chainOne confirmation, or accept after the network shows the payment
A medium purchaseA few confirmations
A high-value purchase on a proof-of-work chainSix or more confirmations
Chains with absolute finalityWait for the finality signal
A small, low-hash-rate chainMany more confirmations, or avoid large payments

Cost of an attack versus the sale

Change the sale value and the attacker's cost to reverse. If the cost is below the value, waiting longer is wise. (Teaching model.)

Adjust Sale value (rupees), Attacker cost to reverse (rupees) and see Attack profit if it succeeds (rupees), Attack cost divided by sale value change.

Tip

Think like an attacker: would it ever be worth reversing this sale? If the sale value is far below the cost of reversing it, the risk is low.

Check what you just learned

1. For a very small payment on a large network you might:
  • Wait 100 blocks
  • Ask for cash
  • Refuse payment
  • Accept one confirmation (correct)

The risk is low compared with the inconvenience.

Key terms: flip and sort

Fork
A split in the chain
Orphan block
A valid block that lost a temporary fork
Reorganisation
Switching to a heavier branch
Soft fork
A backward-compatible rule tightening
Hard fork
A non-backward-compatible change
Replay attack
Reusing a valid transaction on another chain
keyPoints: Choose confirmations by value at stake and chain security.
If attacking costs more than the sale is worth, risk is low.

modules.title: Designing trust
modules.summary: Putting it all together: choosing mechanisms, reading chain designs critically and writing a rulebook.
modules.outcome: You can compare consensus designs for a use case, write consensus rules for a consortium and read claims about a chain with a critical eye.
modules.intro: The last module is about judgement. You will compare real designs, write the rules for a small network and practise asking the questions that separate a robust design from a marketing claim.

topics.title: Choosing a design
topics.html:
Three scenarios
ScenarioLikely designReason
A public currency for strangersPublic chain with PoW or PoSNo trusted identities; security from cost
A bank consortiumPermissioned chain with BFT votingKnown participants, fast finality, accountability
An alumni register run by one schoolA normal databaseOne trusted keeper is enough

Common mistakes

  • Choosing a blockchain because it sounds modern.
  • Choosing proof of work for a group of known institutions.
  • Ignoring governance: who can change the rules, and how?

Check what you just learned

1. A group of ten known banks need a shared settlement ledger. The most sensible consensus is:
  • BFT-style voting among the banks (correct)
  • Proof of work with anonymous miners
  • No consensus
  • Random choice

Identified participants can vote and finalise quickly.

Check what you just learned

1. When one trusted party keeps the record, the best choice is often:
  • A public blockchain
  • A normal database (correct)
  • Proof of work
  • A token

Do not add complexity without a benefit.
keyPoints: Pick the simplest mechanism that gives the trust you need.
Governance matters as much as the algorithm.

topics.title: Writing consensus rules
topics.html:
A consortium chain needs a written rulebook. The technical protocol answers 'how do we agree?', while the rulebook answers 'who may take part, who decides changes and what happens when someone breaks the rules?'.

Parts of a rulebook
PartQuestions
ParticipantsWho can join, how are they approved, how can they leave?
Block proposalWho proposes, in what order, how often?
ValidationWhat must every validator check?
FinalityHow many signatures finalise a block?
Faults and forksWhat happens when validators are offline or misbehave?
UpgradesHow are rules changed and announced?
Worked example

A small rulebook line

A five-validator network.

  1. A block is final when at least 4 of 5 validators sign it.
  2. A validator that signs two conflicting blocks is suspended pending review.
  3. If fewer than 4 validators are online, the ledger pauses rather than risk disagreement.

Answer. Rules that say what happens in bad cases are as important as the happy path.

Good rulebook habits

  • Use numbers: quorum sizes, timeouts, notice periods.
  • Plan for failure: who acts if the proposer is silent?
  • Include an upgrade path.
  • Keep personal data off the shared ledger.
  • Write it so that a new member can read it in one sitting.

Check what you just learned

1. Why should a rulebook say what happens when too few validators are online?
  • To waste time
  • Because validators like rules
  • Because the network must choose safety or liveness in advance (correct)
  • It is a legal formality only

A pause may be safer than a split.

Check what you just learned

1. A good rulebook includes:
  • Only slogans
  • Secret rules
  • No upgrade path
  • Numbers and fault procedures (correct)

Clear and testable.
keyPoints: A rulebook covers participants, proposal, validation, finality, faults and upgrades.
Plan for failure in advance.

topics.title: Reading claims critically
topics.html:
Claims and questions
ClaimAsk
Our chain does 100,000 transactions per secondUnder what conditions, with how many validators, and measured in a real network?
Fully decentralisedHow many entities control most of the validators or hash power?
UnhackableWhich parts have been audited, and what attacks were considered?
Instant finalityWhat are the assumptions, and what happens if one third are offline?
Green and sustainableCompared with what, and measured how?

A reader's checklist

  1. Is the design described in a clear paper or documentation?
  2. Have independent researchers reviewed it?
  3. Has it survived real use and attacks?
  4. Who benefits if you believe the claim?
  5. Is the claim measured or only promised?
Watch out

Performance numbers measured in a lab with a handful of well-connected servers say little about a global open network. Look for real-world, independent measurements.

Check what you just learned

1. When a chain claims huge throughput, what is a good first question?
  • How was it measured and under what conditions? (correct)
  • What colour is the logo?
  • Who is the CEO?
  • Is it popular?

Conditions matter.

Check what you just learned

1. Which claim most deserves scepticism?
  • A documented audit
  • Unhackable (correct)
  • Open code
  • A clear whitepaper

No system is perfectly secure.

Key terms: flip and sort

Permissioned
Only approved participants take part
Rulebook
The written governance of a network
Quorum
Number of votes needed to decide
Liveness
The network keeps making progress
Safety
The network never finalises conflicting blocks
Governance
How rules are decided and changed
keyPoints: Ask how a claim was measured and who is affected.
Lab figures differ from open-network reality.
